title: Malta Year 8 Math — All 19 Chapters: Basic
question: Can you do one quick step from each of the nineteen chapters?
intro:
**Basic:** one step from each chapter, two questions per chapter.

**Chapters:**

- Q1–2: Chapter 1 Directed Numbers
- Q3–4: Chapter 2 Number Work
- Q5–6: Chapter 3 Angles
- Q7–8: Chapter 4 Fractions
- Q9–10: Chapter 5 Decimals
- Q11–12: Chapter 6 Percentages
- Q13–14: Chapter 7 Ratio
- Q15–16: Chapter 8 Algebra
- Q17–18: Chapter 9 Sequences
- Q19–20: Chapter 10 Circles
- Q21–22: Chapter 11 Perimeter & Area
- Q23–24: Chapter 12 Surface Area & Nets
- Q25–26: Chapter 13 Graphs
- Q27–28: Chapter 14 Statistics
- Q29–30: Chapter 15 Probability
- Q31–32: Chapter 16 Constructions
- Q33–34: Chapter 17 Transformations
- Q35–36: Chapter 18 Real-life Problems
- Q37–38: Chapter 19 Logo

questions.title: Ch 1 Directed Numbers · Warmer by 8
questions.prompt:
At night the temperature is \(-3\,^\circ\text{C}\).

By noon it is 8 degrees warmer.

What is the temperature at noon?
questions.figure_alt: A thermometer from −5 to 10 °C. The night temperature −3 is marked; an arrow goes 8 degrees up to a question mark.
questions.solution:
Warmer means move **up** the thermometer:

\[-3 + 8 = \boxed{5}\]

\(-11\) moves 8 the wrong way: warmer is up, not down.

questions.title: Ch 1 Directed Numbers · Below zero
questions.prompt: Work out \(-4 - 5\).
questions.figure_alt: Number line from −10 to 2. Start at −4, five hops to the left, ending at a question mark.
questions.solution:
Start at \(-4\) and move 5 to the **left**:

\[-4 - 5 = \boxed{-9}\]

\(1\) adds the 5 instead of taking it away; \(-1\) takes 4 from 5 and forgets the start is below zero.

questions.title: Ch 2 Number Work · Multiply before adding
questions.prompt: Work out \(3 + 4\times2\).
questions.figure_alt: Three orange dots plus four boxes with two blue dots each, then equals a question mark.
questions.solution:
BIDMAS: multiply first.

\[\begin{aligned} 3 + 4\times2 &= 3 + 8 \\ &= \boxed{11} \end{aligned}\]

\(14\) adds first, as if it were \((3 + 4)\times2\).

questions.title: Ch 2 Number Work · Square number
questions.prompt: Work out \(6^2\).
questions.figure_alt: A 6 by 6 grid of small squares; how many small squares is the question.
questions.solution:
A square number is a square of dots:

\[\begin{aligned} 6^2 &= 6\times6 \\ &= \boxed{36} \end{aligned}\]

\(12\) is \(6\times2\), not \(6\times6\).

questions.title: Ch 3 Angles · Straight line
questions.prompt:
Two angles sit on a straight line.

One is \(130^\circ\).

Find the other angle.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line with a ray from a point on it. The left angle is 130°; the right angle is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Angles on a straight line add up to \(180^\circ\):

\[180^\circ - 130^\circ = \boxed{50^\circ}\]

\(230^\circ\) uses \(360^\circ\), which is for angles around a point.

questions.title: Ch 3 Angles · Triangle
questions.prompt:
A triangle has angles \(60^\circ\) and \(75^\circ\).

Find the third angle.
questions.figure_alt: A triangle with angles 60° and 75° marked; the top angle is a question mark.
questions.solution:
The angles in a triangle add up to \(180^\circ\):

\[180^\circ - 60^\circ - 75^\circ = \boxed{45^\circ}\]

\(225^\circ\) takes them from \(360^\circ\); a triangle uses \(180^\circ\).

questions.title: Ch 4 Fractions · Slices of pizza
questions.prompt:
A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices.

You eat 3 slices and a friend eats 2 slices.

What fraction of the pizza is eaten?
questions.figure_alt: A pizza in 8 slices: 3 orange slices (you), 2 green slices (a friend); the eaten fraction is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Same size slices, so add the tops:

\[\frac{3}{8} + \frac{2}{8} = \boxed{\frac{5}{8}}\]

\(\frac{5}{16}\) adds the bottoms too, but the pizza still has 8 slices, not 16.

questions.title: Ch 4 Fractions · Fraction of an amount
questions.figure_alt: Twenty dots in four equal boxes of five; three boxes are shaded and labelled with a question mark.
questions.solution:
Split 20 into 4 equal groups, then take 3 of them:

\[20\div4 = 5\]

\[5\times3 = \boxed{15}\]

\(5\) is only one quarter; you need three quarters.

questions.title: Ch 5 Decimals · Adding money
questions.figure_alt: A 2 euro and a 50 cent coin, plus a 1 euro, 20 cent and 10 cent coin, equals a question mark.
questions.solution:
Line up the decimal points:

\[2.50 + 1.30 = \boxed{3.80}\]

- The answer is €3.80.
- \(3.53\) or \(2.80\) come from adding digits that are not in the same place.

questions.title: Ch 5 Decimals · Times 10
questions.prompt: Work out \(0.36\times10\).
questions.figure_alt: A place-value table: 0.36 in the top row; arrows move each digit one place left into a row of question marks.
questions.solution:
Every digit moves one place to the left:

\[0.36\times10 = \boxed{3.6}\]

\(0.360\) only adds a zero; the value does not change, so it cannot be ten times bigger.

questions.title: Ch 6 Percentages · Ten percent
questions.figure_alt: A bar for €70 cut into 10 equal blocks; the first block (10%) is a question mark.
questions.solution:
\(10\%\) is one block out of 10:

\[70\div10 = \boxed{7}\]

- So \(10\%\) of €70 is €7.
- \(60\) takes 10 away; a percentage is a part, not a subtraction.

questions.title: Ch 6 Percentages · Percent of a grid
questions.prompt:
The grid has 100 equal squares.

What percentage of the grid is shaded?
questions.figure_alt: A 10 by 10 grid with 3 full columns and 7 more squares shaded blue.
questions.solution:
- Per cent means out of 100.
- Count: 3 full columns and 7 more.

\[30 + 7 = 37\]

\[\frac{37}{100} = \boxed{37\%}\]

\(63\%\) counts the white squares.

questions.title: Ch 7 Ratio · Sharing
questions.prompt:
Share 20 sweets in the ratio \(1 : 3\).

How many sweets are in the bigger share?
questions.figure_alt: A bar model: one orange box for the smaller share, three blue boxes for the bigger share, 20 sweets in all.
questions.solution:
There are \(1 + 3 = 4\) equal parts:

\[20\div4 = 5\]

\[5\times3 = \boxed{15}\]

\(5\) is the smaller share; \(6.67\) splits 20 into 3 parts, but the ratio has 4 parts.

questions.title: Ch 7 Ratio · Simplest form
questions.prompt: Write the ratio \(12 : 8\) in its simplest form.
questions.figure_alt: Twelve red counters in 3 groups of 4 and eight blue counters in 2 groups of 4.
questions.solution:
The HCF of 12 and 8 is 4:

\[12\div4 = 3\]

\[8\div4 = 2\]

\[\boxed{3 : 2}\]

- \(6 : 4\) is the same ratio, but both can still be halved.
- \(2 : 3\) swaps the order.

questions.title: Ch 8 Algebra · Solve
questions.figure_alt: A balance: a bag x and 7 cubes on the left, 12 cubes on the right.
questions.solution:
Take 7 from both sides, so the scale stays balanced:

\[x + 7 = 12\]

\[x = 12 - 7\]

\[x = \boxed{5}\]

\(19\) adds 7 instead of taking it away.

questions.title: Ch 8 Algebra · Substitute
questions.prompt: Work out \(3x + 2\) when \(x = 4\).
questions.figure_alt: A function machine: 4 goes in, times 3, plus 2, and a question mark comes out.
questions.solution:
Put 4 in place of \(x\):

\[\begin{aligned} 3\times4 + 2 &= 12 + 2 \\ &= \boxed{14} \end{aligned}\]

\(36\) reads \(3x\) as 34 — but \(3x\) means \(3\times x\).

questions.title: Ch 9 Sequences · Matchstick pattern
questions.prompt:
Pattern 1 uses 4 matchsticks, pattern 2 uses 7 and pattern 3 uses 10.

How many matchsticks does pattern 4 use?
questions.figure_alt: Matchstick squares in a row: 1, 2 and 3 squares using 4, 7 and 10 sticks; pattern 4 is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Each new square adds 3 sticks:

\[10 + 3 = \boxed{13}\]

\(16\) counts 4 sticks for the new square, but it shares one side with the square before.

questions.title: Ch 9 Sequences · Term rule
questions.prompt:
The rule for term number \(n\) is \(2n + 1\).

Find the 10th term.
questions.figure_alt: A table: n = 1, 2, 3 gives terms 3, 5, 7 (each +2); n = 10 gives a question mark. The rule is 2n + 1.
questions.solution:
Put \(n = 10\) into the rule:

\[\begin{aligned} 2\times10 + 1 &= 20 + 1 \\ &= \boxed{21} \end{aligned}\]

\(12\) reads \(2n\) as 2 + n; \(2n\) means \(2\times n\).

questions.title: Ch 10 Circles · Diameter
questions.prompt:
A circle has radius 7 cm.

Find its diameter.
questions.figure_alt: A circle with a radius of 7 cm drawn from the centre and a dashed diameter across it.
questions.solution:
The diameter goes right across, so it is two radii:

\[\begin{aligned} d &= 2r \\ &= 2\times7 \\ &= \boxed{14 \text{ cm}} \end{aligned}\]

\(3.5\) halves the radius; the diameter is double, not half.

questions.title: Ch 10 Circles · Circumference
questions.prompt:
A circle has diameter 10 cm.

Use \(\pi \approx 3.14\) to find its circumference.
questions.figure_alt: A circle of diameter 10 cm rolled out into a straight line a little more than 3 diameters long.
questions.solution:
The circumference is about 3.14 diameters:

\[\begin{aligned} C &= \pi d \\ &\approx 3.14\times10 \\ &= \boxed{31.4 \text{ cm}} \end{aligned}\]

\(314\) multiplies by 100; \(78.5\) is the area \(\pi r^2\), not the distance round.

questions.title: Ch 11 Perimeter & Area · Rectangle area
questions.prompt:
A rectangle is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide.

Find its area.
questions.figure_alt: A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle split into 1 cm squares.
questions.solution:
Rows of squares:

\[\begin{aligned} A &= l\times w \\ &= 6\times4 \\ &= \boxed{24 \text{ cm}^2} \end{aligned}\]

\(20\) is the perimeter (the distance round), not the area.

questions.title: Ch 11 Perimeter & Area · Triangle area
questions.prompt:
A triangle has base 6 cm and height 4 cm.

Find its area.
questions.figure_alt: A triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm drawn inside a dashed 6 by 4 rectangle on a grid.
questions.solution:
A triangle is half of its rectangle:

\[\begin{aligned} A &= \tfrac{1}{2}bh \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2}\times6\times4 \\ &= \boxed{12 \text{ cm}^2} \end{aligned}\]

\(24\) forgets the half.

questions.title: Ch 12 Surface Area & Nets · Cube surface area
questions.prompt:
A cube has edges of 2 cm.

Find its surface area.
questions.figure_alt: A cube with 2 cm edges and its net of six squares, each 2 by 2.
questions.solution:
6 square faces, each:

\[\begin{aligned} 2\times2 &= 4 \text{ cm}^2 \\ SA &= 6a^2 \\ &= 6\times4 \\ &= \boxed{24 \text{ cm}^2} \end{aligned}\]

\(8\) is the volume \(2\times2\times2\); surface area covers the outside.

questions.title: Ch 12 Surface Area & Nets · Cuboid volume
questions.prompt:
A cuboid is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high.

Find its volume.
questions.figure_alt: A cuboid 5 by 3 by 2 built from 1 cm cubes.
questions.solution:
Count the cubes, layer by layer:

\[\begin{aligned} V &= lwh \\ &= 5\times3\times2 \\ &= \boxed{30 \text{ cm}^3} \end{aligned}\]

\(10\) adds the edges; volume multiplies them.

questions.title: Ch 13 Graphs · Coordinates
questions.prompt: What are the coordinates of point A?
questions.figure_alt: A coordinate grid with point A plotted.
questions.solution:
From 0 go 3 across, then 2 up:

\[\boxed{(3, 2)}\]

\((2, 3)\) reads up before across.

questions.title: Ch 13 Graphs · Line value
questions.prompt:
The line is \(y = 2x + 1\).

Find \(y\) when \(x = 3\).
questions.figure_alt: The line y = 2x + 1 on a grid; a dashed line from x = 3 goes up to the line at a question mark.
questions.solution:
Put \(x = 3\) into the rule:

\[\begin{aligned} y &= 2\times3 + 1 \\ &= 6 + 1 \\ &= \boxed{7} \end{aligned}\]

\(9\) adds before multiplying: multiply first.

questions.title: Ch 14 Statistics · Mode
questions.prompt: Find the mode of \(3, 5, 5, 6, 5, 8\).
questions.figure_alt: A dot plot of 3, 5, 5, 6, 5, 8: the column above 5 is the tallest.
questions.solution:
The mode is the value that appears most often: 5 appears 3 times.

\[\text{mode} = \boxed{5}\]

\(3\) is how many times 5 appears, not the value itself.

questions.title: Ch 14 Statistics · Mean
questions.prompt: Find the mean of \(3, 7, 8, 6\).
questions.figure_alt: A bar chart of 3, 7, 8 and 6; the mean, the level height, is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Add them, then share equally between the 4 values:

\[3 + 7 + 8 + 6 = 24\]

\[24\div4 = \boxed{6}\]

\(24\) is the total; the mean shares it out.

questions.title: Ch 15 Probability · Bag of counters
questions.prompt:
A bag has 3 red and 5 blue counters.

One counter is taken without looking.

What is the probability that it is red?
questions.figure_alt: A bag with 3 red and 5 blue counters inside.
questions.solution:
3 red out of \(3 + 5 = 8\) counters:

\[P(\text{red}) = \boxed{\frac{3}{8}}\]

\(\frac{3}{5}\) compares red with blue; a probability compares with **all** the counters.

questions.title: Ch 15 Probability · Not blue
questions.prompt:
A spinner has 8 equal parts: 3 blue and 5 yellow.

What is the probability that it does **not** land on blue?
questions.figure_alt: A spinner with 8 equal parts, 3 blue and 5 yellow, and an arrow pointer.
questions.solution:
\[\begin{aligned} P(\text{not blue}) &= 1 - \frac{3}{8} \\ &= \boxed{\frac{5}{8}} \end{aligned}\]

- \(\frac{3}{8}\) is P(blue) itself.
- \(\frac{5}{3}\) is more than 1, and no probability is more than 1.

questions.title: Ch 16 Constructions · Can it be a triangle?
questions.prompt: Which three lengths can make a triangle?
questions.figure_alt: A base of 8 cm with compass arcs of 3 cm and 4 cm from its ends; the arcs leave a gap and never meet.
questions.solution_title: The two short sides must reach
questions.solution:
The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest:

\[4 + 5 = 9\]

\[9 > 7\]

- So \(\boxed{4 \text{ cm}, 5 \text{ cm}, 7 \text{ cm}}\) works.
- In the others the short sides are too short: \(3 + 4 = 7\), \(2 + 3 = 5\) and \(1 + 2 = 3\), each less than the longest side.

questions.title: Ch 16 Constructions · Angle bisector
questions.prompt:
An angle of \(70^\circ\) is bisected.

What is each smaller angle?
questions.figure_alt: An angle of 70° with a dashed bisector splitting it into two equal angles marked with question marks.
questions.solution:
Bisect means cut into two equal halves:

\[70^\circ\div2 = \boxed{35^\circ}\]

\(140^\circ\) doubles instead of halving.

questions.title: Ch 17 Transformations · Reflection
questions.prompt:
Reflect the point \(P(3, 2)\) in the \(y\)-axis.

Where is its image?
questions.figure_alt: A grid with the y-axis as a mirror; point P(3, 2) on the right and a dashed arrow to a question mark on the left.
questions.solution:
The \(y\)-axis is the mirror: \(x\) changes sign, \(y\) stays.

\[(3, 2) \to \boxed{(-3, 2)}\]

\((3, -2)\) reflects in the \(x\)-axis instead.

questions.title: Ch 17 Transformations · Translation
questions.prompt:
Translate the point \((1, 2)\) by \(\binom{4}{1}\): 4 right and 1 up.

Where does it go?
questions.figure_alt: A grid with point (1, 2), an arrow 4 to the right and an arrow 1 up ending at a question mark.
questions.solution:
Add 4 to \(x\) and 1 to \(y\):

\[(1 + 4,\ 2 + 1) = \boxed{(5, 3)}\]

\((4, 1)\) is the move itself, not where the point lands.

questions.title: Ch 18 Real-life Problems · Change
questions.prompt:
The bill is €6.35.

You pay with a €10 note.

How much change do you get?
questions.figure_alt: A receipt with a total of €6.35 next to a €10 note; the change is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Change = money paid − cost:

\[10.00 - 6.35 = \boxed{3.65}\]

- The change is €3.65.
- \(4.75\) subtracts each digit the wrong way round.

questions.title: Ch 18 Real-life Problems · Journey time
questions.prompt:
A bus leaves at 09:40 and arrives at 10:15.

How many minutes is the journey?
questions.figure_alt: Two clocks: 9:40 and 10:15, with an arrow between them marked question mark minutes.
questions.solution:
Count up to the hour, then on:

\[09{:}40 \to 10{:}00 = 20 \text{ min}\]

\[10{:}00 \to 10{:}15 = 15 \text{ min}\]

\[20 + 15 = \boxed{35 \text{ min}}\]

\(75\) subtracts 1015 − 940 as ordinary numbers, but an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.

questions.title: Ch 19 Logo · Square turn
questions.prompt:
The turtle draws a square.

It walks forward 50 steps and turns right, 4 times.

In Logo this is `REPEAT 4 [FD 50 RT ?]`.

- `FD 50` means move forward 50 steps (a length).
- `RT ?` means turn right by ? degrees (an angle).

How many degrees is each turn?
questions.figure_alt: A square walked clockwise from the start: arrows 1 to 4 are forward 50 steps; at each corner a dashed straight-on line and a right turn marked with a question mark.
questions.solution:
The turtle turns by how much its direction changes:

- Straight on is a turn of \(0^\circ\).
- Turning round to walk back is \(180^\circ\).
- A square's corner is \(90^\circ\), so the turn is

\[180^\circ - 90^\circ = \boxed{90^\circ}\]

Check: 4 turns make one full spin, \(4\times90^\circ = 360^\circ\), so the turtle ends facing the way it started.

\(4\) is the number of sides, not the angle.

questions.title: Ch 19 Logo · Triangle commands
questions.prompt:
The turtle draws an equilateral triangle (every inside angle is 60°).

It walks forward 60 steps and turns right, 3 times.

- `FD 60` means move forward 60 steps (a length).
- `RT` means turn right by that many degrees (an angle).

Which commands draw it?
questions.figure_alt: A triangle hanging below the start line, walked with right turns: arrows 1 to 3 are forward 60 steps; at corner B the dashed straight-on line, the inside angle 60° and the right turn marked with a question mark.
questions.solution:
Look at corner B in the picture (the turtle walks A → B → C → A):

- Straight on (the dashed line) is a turn of \(0^\circ\).
- Turning round to walk back to the start is \(180^\circ\).
- The new side is \(60^\circ\) away from walking back, so the turn is

\[180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\]

Check: \(3\times120^\circ = 360^\circ\), one full spin, so the path closes.

\[\boxed{\texttt{REPEAT 3 [FD 60 RT 120]}}\]

`RT 60` uses the inside angle: the turtle turns too little and needs 6 sides to close (a hexagon). `FD 120` makes sides of 120 steps, not 60.

takeaway:
- Draw it first: a picture shows which rule to use.
- Check that the answer makes sense in the picture.
